name: Carthaginian army under Hannibal (218-202 BC)

weightNotes.aggression: Invaded Italy over the Alps in 218 and sought battle three times in three years (Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae; Second Punic War pages). Not higher because after Cannae he never marched on Rome and from 207 sat 'undefeated but ineffective' in Bruttium (Zama page).
weightNotes.maneuver: Operational manoeuvre was the method: the Alpine crossing, the march round Fabius, and the Trasimene ambush, 'widely considered a unique occurrence' of a whole army destroyed by ambush (Trasimene page; Lazenby, Hannibal's War).
weightNotes.flanking: Every great victory was an envelopment: Mago's 2,000 hidden in a watercourse hit the Roman rear at the Trebia; at Cannae the Africans on the wings closed on the Roman flanks while the cavalry took the rear (Cannae, Trebia pages). Near maximum.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Saguntum (219) took eight months; in Italy he had no siege train and never besieged Rome; Hasdrubal was bringing 'siege equipment' when destroyed at the Metaurus (Metaurus page). Field battle was the strategy.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Held forces out of sight or out of the fight until the decisive moment: Mago's ambush party at the Trebia, the uncommitted African infantry at Cannae, the veteran third line kept 200 m back at Zama (Zama page). Moderate fraction.
weightNotes.scouting: Hannibal read Roman commanders and ground well (Flaminius lured into the Trasimene defile; Numidian screens). Lowered because neither Hannibal nor Hasdrubal detected Nero's forced march before the Metaurus (Metaurus page).
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Hannibal's own army held to destruction rather than withdraw: Zama 202 BC, about 100% (Polybius: 20,000 killed and as many captured, 'the entire Carthaginian army', Zama page); Metaurus 207 BC, Hasdrubal's army routed after being outflanked with 15,400 killed or captured and Hasdrubal dead (army size only from ancient figures, so no reliable share; Metaurus page). In victory it absorbed losses without breaking: Cannae 216 BC, about 11% (Polybius 5,700 dead of roughly 50,000, Cannae page) while the centre gave ground on orders. Allied first-line and new levies at Zama broke earlier (no figure). 0.6: holds until largely destroyed.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Libyan heavy foot, Iberian and Gallic line infantry, Balearic slingers, Iberian and Gallic heavy horse, Numidian javelin horse and elephants, each with a defined role (Military of Carthage, Cannae pages).
weightNotes.initiative: Subordinates (Mago, Maharbal, Hasdrubal of the cavalry) executed timed independent parts of the plan, but the system depended on Hannibal personally; other Carthaginian generals in Spain and Africa were repeatedly beaten (Zama page). Middling.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Lived off Italy for 15 years with almost no seaborne resupply; lost heavily crossing the Alps (13,000 men in the two-month campaign, Alps page); Fabius's strategy targeted his foraging (Fabian strategy page). Operations ignored supply limits.

summary: A multinational professional army (African, Iberian, Gallic and Numidian contingents, with elephants) commanded personally by Hannibal. It invaded Italy overland, lived off the country, and sought battle on ground Hannibal chose: Numidian horse lured the Romans across the Trebia, the whole army ambushed a consular army on the march at Lake Trasimene, and at Cannae a deliberately yielding infantry centre drew the Roman mass forward while African infantry closed the flanks and the cavalry sealed the rear. It lacked a siege train and the political base to convert victories into the surrender of Rome.
whyItWorked: Superior cavalry and a commander who used terrain, deception and timing better than any opponent until Scipio; the yielding centre at Cannae (216 BC, at least 67,500 Romans killed or captured per the Zama page summary) is the classic double envelopment. Mixed contingents were given tasks that matched their arms, and the army stayed loyal through 15 years far from home.
whereItFailed: Could not take fortified cities or force Rome to negotiate; the Fabian strategy of shadowing and denying forage wore it down. When Hasdrubal's relief army was caught and destroyed at the Metaurus (207 BC, 15,400 killed or captured), Hannibal was confined to Bruttium. At Zama (202 BC) Scipio had the better cavalry (Masinissa's Numidians); the Carthaginian horse was driven off, returned Roman cavalry hit the veteran line in the rear and the army was destroyed.
